title: Conjunctions & connectives
examples: What is the difference between a coordinating and subordinating conjunction?
Can I use commas when I join two sentences?

explain.say: Today we are learning how to join sentences together smoothly. We use special words called conjunctions for this. These words help your writing flow nicely.
First we look at coordinating conjunctions. These join two equal ideas together. Remember the word FANBOYS for these words.
For example, I like apples, and my friend likes bananas. We used 'and' to join two things. Both ideas are just as important.
Next we look at subordinating conjunctions. These join a main idea to a less important one. They show a relationship like time or reason.
For example, we played outside because the sun was shining. 'Because' tells us the reason for playing outside. The main idea is playing outside.
In real life, you use these words all the time. Think about why you are wearing your coat today. You wear it because it is cold outside.

faq.q: Do I always need a comma when I join sentences?
faq.a: You usually need a comma when you use a coordinating conjunction like 'and' or 'but'. For example, put a comma before the joining word.
asks: Do I always put a comma?
When do I use punctuation with conjunctions?

faq.q: Is there a difference between 'so' and 'because'?
faq.a: Yes, 'because' shows the reason for something. 'So' shows the result or the effect of something happening.
These words connect a main idea to a supporting idea. Some common ones are 'although', 'because', and 'when'.
asks: What words start a dependent clause?

faq.q: Can I use 'and' to join two very different ideas?
faq.a: Yes, you can use 'and' if both ideas are equally important. For example, I read books and I play sports.
Cohesion means that your writing sticks together nicely. It means your ideas flow smoothly from one to the next.
asks: How do I make my writing connect?

facts: Coordinating conjunctions join two equal parts of a sentence.
The FANBOYS acronym stands for For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.
Subordinating conjunctions show a relationship like time or cause.
A comma is often needed before a coordinating conjunction.

quiz.say: She was tired, so she went to bed early.
quiz.show: Tired, so she went to bed early.
quiz.why: The word 'so' correctly shows the result of being tired.

wrong.0: Using 'and' suggests two separate, equally weighted facts, not a cause-and-effect link.
wrong.1: Using 'yet' suggests a surprising contrast, which is not the relationship shown here.
wrong.3: Using 'because' suggests being tired is the reason she went to bed, which is less direct than showing the result.

quiz.say: I ate my lunch because I was hungry.
quiz.show: I ate lunch because I was hungry.
quiz.why: The word 'because' correctly introduces the reason for eating lunch.

wrong.0: Using 'and' treats the hunger and the eating as two separate, unrelated facts.
wrong.1: Using 'but' suggests a contrast, when in fact the hunger is the direct cause.
wrong.3: Using 'so' would imply eating lunch was the result of being hungry, which reverses the logic.

quiz.say: The lights went out when the storm hit.
quiz.why: The word 'when' correctly shows that the lights going out happened at the time the storm hit.

wrong.0: Using 'because' suggests the storm hitting was the reason the lights went out, which is possible but 'when' is more precise for timing.
wrong.2: Using 'so' implies the storm hitting was the result of the lights going out.
wrong.3: Using 'and' just lists two events without showing the time relationship between them.
